scenes.title: Propositions and Truth Tables
scenes.summary: Switch the connective and watch the new column fill in while the P, Q columns stay fixed. Compare the shaded P \to Q column with its contrapositive \lnot Q \to \lnot P row by row — identical in all four rows. The converse Q \to P, though, splits off in the (T, F) row.

scenes.title: Universal and Existential Quantifiers
scenes.summary: A game on the number line: the challenger names x, and you answer with the bigger point y = x + 1 — \forall x \,\exists y \,(y > x). Swap the quantifier order and the same game collapses. The \varepsilon-\delta line is exactly this pattern, with \delta = \varepsilon/2 answering f(t) = 2t.

scenes.title: Direct Proof
scenes.summary: The sum of two rationals r_1 = \frac{p_1}{q_1}, r_2 = \frac{p_2}{q_2} on a number line, with the computation \frac{p_1 q_2 + p_2 q_1}{q_1 q_2} running straight from hypothesis to conclusion — that is a direct proof.

scenes.title: Proof by Contrapositive
scenes.summary: The n = 1..12 grid where the n^2-even rows are exactly the n-even rows — where the direct proof of "n^2 even \Rightarrow n even" stalls, the contrapositive "odd n \Rightarrow odd n^2" opens up through (2k+1)^2 = 2(2k^2+2k)+1.

scenes.title: Proof by Contradiction
scenes.summary: Suppose the primes p_1, \ldots, p_k were all there are — the chips show the list, P = p_1 \cdots p_k, and N = P+1. N is divisible by no prime on the list (remainder 1) yet has a prime factor, and that factor is off the list — a contradiction. At k = 6, N = 30031 = 59 \times 509 is composite and the proof still stands, teaching the shape of contradiction (assume \lnot P → contradiction → P).

scenes.title: Proof by Cases and Existence Proofs
scenes.summary: Moving the point (x, y) shades its quadrant and unfolds that case's computation of |xy| = |x|\cdot|y| — the four cases (and the axes) cover the whole plane. And from c = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}} two branches fork and rejoin at "irrational a, b exist with a^b rational" without ever revealing which branch is true — the flavor of non-constructive existence.

scenes.title: Counterexamples and If and Only If
scenes.summary: Watch a single counterexample demolish a universal claim, tested on four false claims — every prime is odd, 4 \mid n^2 \Rightarrow 4 \mid n, sums of irrationals are irrational, |x| = |y| \Rightarrow x = y. Slide n and flip the hypothesis and conclusion lights until \lnot(\forall x\, P(x)) = \exists x\, \lnot P(x) feels mechanical. The mirror skill — proving each arrow of P \iff Q separately — is carried out in the problems.

scenes.title: Strong Induction
scenes.summary: Draw the factorization tree of n = 30 and strong induction explains itself — the splits drop to much smaller numbers like 15 and 2, not to n - 1 = 29. Slide n, watch the tree redraw, and follow the induction step that assumes all of P(2), \dots, P(n-1) at once; the weak hypothesis P(n-1) alone can never reach the factors.

scenes.title: Equivalence Relations
scenes.summary: Congruence modulo n as an equivalence relation: the three axioms — reflexive, symmetric, transitive — are brute-force verified on every element, pair, and triple of U = \{0, \dots, 3n-1\}, and the classes [r] = \{r, r+n, r+2n\} visibly partition the set as n slides.

scenes.title: Proofs about Composite Functions
scenes.summary: Proofs about composite functions, tested on concrete tables: g \circ f injective forces f injective, g \circ f surjective forces g surjective — and the arrow diagrams show exactly why the converses fail (g need not be injective, f need not be surjective). For bijections, (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} is computed out loud.

scenes.title: Natural Numbers and Induction
scenes.summary: The natural numbers start from the Peano axioms: P(1) plus P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1) yields P(n) for every natural number n — addition and multiplication are also defined recursively, and this one principle proves infinitely many statements at once.

scenes.title: The Binomial Theorem
scenes.summary: The binomial theorem (x+y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^{n-k}y^k proved by induction — Pascal's identity \binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}=\binom{n+1}{k} is the inductive step, and row n of Pascal's triangle is drawn live.

scenes.title: Integers and Rationals
scenes.summary: Integers arise as equivalence classes of natural pairs with (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c, and rationals as classes of integer pairs with (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff ad=bc. The "numbers as equivalence classes" trick returns when the reals are built from the rationals.

scenes.title: √2 is Irrational
scenes.summary: Plotting the rationals p/q with denominator at most N on [1, 2] leaves a hole at \sqrt{2} \approx 1.4142 — no N ever fills it. Proposition 4.4.4: no rational squares to 2.

scenes.title: Density of the Rationals
scenes.summary: Every open interval (x, y) contains a rational: with n = \lfloor 1/(y-x) \rfloor + 1 and m = \lfloor nx \rfloor + 1, x < m/n < y. Watch the rational ticks inside the interval multiply as the denominator cap grows.

scenes.title: Sets and Functions
scenes.summary: See set operations A \cup B, A \cap B, A^c, De Morgan's laws, and injective / surjective / bijective maps as pictures.

scenes.title: The Axiom of Choice
scenes.summary: A function picking one element from each set in a collection — for finite collections no axiom is needed, but for infinite ones this "picking" is itself an axiom. Pick one dot per row.

scenes.title: Zorn's Lemma
scenes.summary: If every chain has an upper bound, a maximal element exists — light up the chains one by one in the divisibility poset of 12's divisors. Equivalent to the axiom of choice, the master key of algebra.

scenes.title: The Supremum Axiom
scenes.summary: Every bounded-above set has a least upper bound \sup S — the axiom filling the gaps in the rationals, twin of the rational-holes scene.

scenes.title: Existence of n-th Roots
scenes.summary: The supremum of \{x \ge 0 : x^n < a\} IS \sqrt[n]{a} — watch the supremum axiom fill a "gap" and manufacture a root.

scenes.title: Countable vs Uncountable
scenes.summary: The rationals fit into a single list; the reals do not — verified by Cantor's diagonal argument.

scenes.title: Cantor's Theorem
scenes.summary: Every set is smaller than its power set — |X| < |\mathcal{P}(X)|. The diagonal-flipped set differs from every row of the list. (This is the theorem itself, not the Cantor "set" scene.)

scenes.title: Groups vs Fields
scenes.summary: A group is reversible moves (associativity, identity, inverses); a field is a world where all four operations work. Includes the subgroup test and (\mathbb{Z},+) vs (\mathbb{Q},+,\times).

scenes.title: Vector Spaces and Isomorphism
scenes.summary: A vector space is an abelian group over a field with scalar multiplication — \mathbb{R}^n, sequence spaces, and spaces of continuous functions are the same structure in different packaging. Move (a, b) and the line y = a+bx and the point (a, b) move together.

scenes.title: Dimension and Rank
scenes.summary: If isomorphism means "same structure", dimension and rank measure its size. Watch the grid get squeezed by a matrix and verify \dim\ker T + \mathrm{rank}\,T = \dim V.

scenes.title: The ε–N Definition
scenes.summary: Watch the moment the whole tail of a sequence fits inside the \varepsilon-band. That N is exactly the N in \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N.

scenes.title: Standard Limits: x^n and x^{1/n}
scenes.summary: x^n sinks to 0 when |x| < 1; x^{1/n} gathers at 1 when x > 0. At x = -1 it oscillates, and for |x| > 1 it diverges. Bernoulli's inequality handles every case.

scenes.title: Sequence and Function Spaces
scenes.summary: \ell^1, \ell^2, \ell^\infty and C[0,1] — vector spaces under pointwise operations, metric spaces via the norm \|x - y\|. A normed space bridges both worlds. Watch the inclusion chain \ell^1 \subset \ell^2 \subset \ell^\infty through x_n = 1/n^\alpha. Completeness of \ell^p and C[0,1] (Banach spaces) is stated as a known theorem only.

scenes.title: Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality
scenes.summary: |\langle x,y\rangle| \le \|x\|\,\|y\| — the inner product never exceeds the product of the norms. Proved from the discriminant of 0 \le \|x-ty\|^2; equality holds exactly for parallel vectors.

scenes.title: Hölder’s Inequality
scenes.summary: \sum |a_k b_k| \le \|a\|_p \|b\|_q (\frac1p + \frac1q = 1) — Cauchy–Schwarz is the case p = q = 2. Proved via Young's inequality.

scenes.title: Why ℝ Has No Holes
scenes.summary: Every term of x_{n+1}=\frac{x_n+2/x_n}{2} is rational, yet the limit \sqrt{2} is not. The rationals \mathbb{Q} have a hole — shown at the idea level, without a full irrationality proof.

scenes.title: Construction of the Real Numbers
scenes.summary: A real number is an equivalence class of Cauchy sequences of rationals. Lengthening the decimal expansion of \sqrt{2} marches rational terms into the hole — the march itself is the real number \sqrt{2}. Completeness is what this construction buys.

scenes.title: A Convergent Subsequence Always Hides Inside
scenes.summary: Every bounded sequence hides a convergent subsequence. Halve the interval and follow the half holding infinitely many terms.

scenes.title: Monotone and Cauchy Sequences
scenes.summary: a_n = 1 - 2^{-n} increases and is bounded above, so it converges to its supremum 1 (monotone convergence). Watch the tail diameter shrink to 0: every convergent sequence is Cauchy.

scenes.title: Lim sup and Lim inf
scenes.summary: Where the suprema and infima of tails settle: for a_n = (-1)^n(1+1/n), \limsup a_n = 1 and \liminf a_n = -1. \limsup a_n = \liminf a_n \iff \lim a_n exists.

scenes.title: Stolz–Cesàro Theorem
scenes.summary: The sequence version of l'Hôpital: if (b_n) is strictly increasing and unbounded and \lim \frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{b_{n+1}-b_n} = L, then \lim \frac{a_n}{b_n} = L. Watch the difference ratio settle at \frac{1}{3} first and the full ratio follow for a_n = 1^2+\cdots+n^2, b_n = n^3.

scenes.title: The ε–δ Definition
scenes.summary: The rigorous meaning of \lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L: no matter how narrow the \varepsilon-band, there is a \delta-band around a where f stays inside it. Check \delta = \varepsilon/2 for f(x) = 2x, a = 1, L = 2.

scenes.title: The Definition of Continuity
scenes.summary: f is continuous at a when \lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a) — the limit and the value must agree. Move the point a; in broken mode the value at one point is lifted and the definition breaks.

scenes.title: Thomae's Function
scenes.summary: The popcorn function f(p/q) = 1/q (reduced), f(x) = 0 (irrational): continuous at every irrational, discontinuous at every rational. Given \varepsilon, only finitely many dots reach height \varepsilon — so near an irrational a \delta can always be found.

scenes.title: Three Faces of Continuity
scenes.summary: Continuity has three faces: the \varepsilon-\delta argument, the sequential test, and preimages of open sets. Placing f(x) = x^2 next to a jump function shows the three faces saying the same thing.

scenes.title: Discontinuities of Monotone Functions
scenes.summary: A monotone function has left and right limits everywhere, so every discontinuity is a jump. Only finitely many jumps can exceed 1/n, so the discontinuities are at most countable — no matter how many there are.

scenes.title: Uniform Continuity
scenes.summary: Uniform continuity demands one \delta that works at every point x — \delta may depend on \varepsilon alone, never on x. Watch the required \delta shrink as x grows for f(x) = x^2, so no single \delta covers all of \mathbb{R}.

scenes.title: You Can't Climb Without Crossing Every Height
scenes.summary: A continuous function on [a,b] must step on every value between f(a) and f(b). Move the target level c and find the crossing \xi.

scenes.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
scenes.summary: A continuous function on a closed interval always attains its max and min. Verify it for f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [-2,2], and see from the open-interval and discontinuous counterexamples that both hypotheses are necessary.

scenes.title: When the Limit Breaks
scenes.summary: f_n(x)=x^n converges at every point of [0,1], yet \sup|f_n-f|=1\not\to 0: not uniformly. Watch the limit break at x=1.

scenes.title: Open and Closed Sets
scenes.summary: A set U is open when every point is an interior point — each point can be wrapped in an \varepsilon-ball. Move the point x and the radius \varepsilon on the line and watch whether the ball stays inside.

scenes.title: Clopen Sets
scenes.summary: Sets that are both open and closed — clopen. In \mathbb{R} only \varnothing and \mathbb{R} qualify (proved in full), but change the ambient space and the same set's fate changes: [0,1] is merely closed in \mathbb{R}, yet clopen inside [0,1]\cup[2,3].

scenes.title: Closure and Boundedness
scenes.summary: Drawing a bar over A gives the closure \overline{A} — the set with its escaped limit points pulled back in. Follow the round-song: closed ⟺ contains its limit points ⟺ equals its closure, and closed + bounded ⟺ compact (Heine-Borel).

scenes.title: Compact Sets
scenes.summary: Compact \iff closed + bounded (Heine–Borel): [0,1] is covered by the first 6 intervals of its open cover, while (0,1] fails at the gap near 0 and [0,\infty) fails at the infinite tail. Sequential compactness via Bolzano–Weierstrass is proved in full; the open-cover definition's equivalence is shown at the idea level.

scenes.title: Topologist's Sine Curve
scenes.summary: The closure of \{(x, \sin(1/x)) : x > 0\} adds the segment \{0\}\times[-1,1] on the y-axis. Connected as the closure of a connected set, yet no path runs from the segment into the curve — the living example of why connected is weaker than path-connected.

scenes.title: Peano Curve
scenes.summary: A continuous map [0,1] \to [0,1]^2 can fill the whole square — recursively repeating the 9-subsquare snake yields uniformly convergent approximations with a surjective continuous limit. Injectivity is impossible (Netto's theorem, proved in full).

scenes.title: Metric Spaces
scenes.summary: Axiomatizing distance generalizes the \varepsilon-ball — the shape of an open ball B(c, r) depends on the metric d. Compare the Euclidean disk, the max-norm square, and the extreme discrete metric.

scenes.title: Contraction Mapping Principle
scenes.summary: A contraction d(Tx,Ty) \le q\,d(x,y) (q<1) on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point — the Picard iterates x_{n+1} = Tx_n tighten inside the error ball \frac{q^n}{1-q}|x_1-x_0|. T(x) = x/2 on (0,1] shows why completeness is essential: a contraction with no fixed point.

scenes.title: Baire Category Theorem
scenes.summary: A complete metric space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense sets — that is the Baire Category Theorem. Dodging the rationals of [0, 1] one by one with nested closed intervals I_k leaves a single irrational point in the intersection, whose lengths shrink to 0.

scenes.title: Baire Class 1 Functions
scenes.summary: Pointwise limits of continuous functions — Baire class 1. Thomae's function T(p/q) = 1/q (reduced), T(x) = 0 (irrational) is the pointwise limit of sums f_n of disjoint tents. T is continuous at irrationals, discontinuous at rationals — a living example of Baire's theorem that the continuity points contain a dense G_\delta.

scenes.title: Length Zero, Points Uncountable
scenes.summary: Deleting middle thirds drives the total length \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n\to 0, yet uncountably many points remain. Uncountability is stated at the idea level only.

scenes.title: The Fat Cantor Set
scenes.summary: What if we dig out less? Removing only length 4^{-n} per interval leaves a set that is compact, nowhere dense and perfect — yet keeps total length \frac12. Measure and topological size are independent notions.

scenes.title: The Cantor Function
scenes.summary: The Devil's staircase: continuous and nondecreasing from 0 to 1, yet constant on every complementary interval, so f' = 0 on a set of total length 1. f(1) - f(0) = 1 \neq \int_0^1 f' — why the FTC needs more than differentiability almost everywhere.

scenes.title: Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem
scenes.summary: When does a family of continuous functions hide a uniformly convergent subsequence? Uniform boundedness plus equicontinuity lets the diagonal argument extract one. Contrast with x^n, where it fails.

scenes.title: Weierstrass Approximation Theorem
scenes.summary: Every continuous function on [0,1] is uniformly approximable by polynomials — watch the Bernstein polynomials B_n(f) close in on f as n grows. The fine estimates of the convergence proof are sketched at the idea level.

scenes.title: Stone–Weierstrass Theorem
scenes.summary: A subalgebra that separates points and contains the constants is uniformly dense — trigonometric polynomials on the circle close in on the triangle wave |x|, with no algebraic polynomial in sight.

scenes.title: Müntz–Szász Theorem
scenes.summary: Approximate \sqrt{x} by least squares and watch the theorem decide: the dense basis \{1, x, \ldots, x^N\} (\lambda_n = n, \sum \frac{1}{n} = \infty) shrinks its error 0.1003 \to 0.0708 \to 0.0544, while the sparse basis \{1, x, x^4, \ldots, x^{N^2}\} (\sum \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} < \infty) stays stuck near 0.16.

scenes.title: The Harmonic Series Diverges
scenes.summary: The partial sums S_n follow \ln n + \gamma upward — very slowly, but without end.

scenes.title: The Euler–Mascheroni Constant
scenes.summary: The harmonic numbers H_n diverge like \ln n, but their gap \gamma_n = H_n - \ln n settles at \gamma \approx 0.5772 — the secret is the convergent series \sum (\frac1n - \ln(1+\frac1n)).

scenes.title: The Basel Problem
scenes.summary: Stack the terms \frac{1}{n^2} as 3D bars and watch the staircase of partial sums approach the plane at \frac{\pi^2}{6} without ever touching it. Why \pi appears at all is only sketched at the idea level.

scenes.title: The Euler Product
scenes.summary: Multiplying \zeta(s) = \sum_{n\ge 1} n^{-s} by (1-2^{-s}) sieves out the even terms, then (1-3^{-s}) removes multiples of 3 — sieving leaves only the product over primes \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}. Watch the partial product over the first k primes approach \zeta(2) = \pi^2/6.

scenes.title: Leibniz Series
scenes.summary: The partial sums overshoot and undershoot \frac{\pi}{4} in turn, closing in from both sides. The gap between two neighboring partial sums is exactly the error bound.

scenes.title: Convergence Tests Toolbox
scenes.summary: When the ratio r_k = a_{k+1}/a_k settles to a limit L < 1, the series converges — watch the ratios dive to 0 and \frac{1}{2} in two series, and \frac{1}{k^2+1} tuck itself under \frac{1}{k^2} for the comparison test.

scenes.title: The Integral Test
scenes.summary: For a decreasing positive function the rectangles lock above and below the curve: \int_1^{N+1} f \le \sum_1^N f(n) \le f(1) + \int_1^{N+1} f — series and improper integral share one fate. Move p to see the p-series fork.

scenes.title: Raabe's Test
scenes.summary: When the ratio drifts to 1 and the ratio test surrenders, the finer quantity R_n = n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1) settles above or below 1 and decides convergence.

scenes.title: Kummer's Test
scenes.summary: Weighting the ratio by a positive auxiliary sequence (p_n), the sign of K_n = p_n\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}} - p_{n+1} decides convergence. p_n = 1 recovers the ratio test, p_n = n recovers Raabe's test.

scenes.title: Cauchy Condensation Test
scenes.summary: Group the terms a_n into blocks [2^n, 2^{n+1}): each block sum is sandwiched between condensed terms 2^n a_{2^n}, so the original and condensed series share their fate.

scenes.title: Telescoping Series
scenes.summary: Split each term into \frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{n+1} and the neighbors cancel each other, leaving only the very first 1 and a vanishing tail.

scenes.title: Geometric Series: Filling the Square
scenes.summary: Fill a unit square by always taking half of what remains: the gap halves at every step and the total becomes 1.

scenes.title: Wallis Product
scenes.summary: Multiply the rational factors in one at a time and watch the running product swing above and below \frac{\pi}{2}, closing in as the swings shrink.

scenes.title: Stirling's Approximation
scenes.summary: On a log scale, n! and the Stirling approximation nearly coincide, and the relative error shrinks like \frac{1}{12n}. Where \pi enters is only sketched at the idea level.

scenes.title: Grandi Series
scenes.summary: The partial sums bounce between 1 and 0 forever, so this series has no sum. \frac{1}{2} is only the average of the partial sums (the Cesàro mean), not a sum of the series.

scenes.title: Dirichlet's Test
scenes.summary: The partial sums of \sin(kx) wobble, trapped inside 1/|\sin(x/2)|, and the 1/n weight sinking to 0 tames them into the convergent series \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sin(nx)}{n} — Dirichlet's test.

scenes.title: Abel's Test
scenes.summary: If \\\sum a_n\ converges and \(b_n)\ is monotone and bounded, then \\\sum a_n b_n\ converges — the companion to Dirichlet's test. The difference: \(b_n)\ need not tend to 0.

scenes.title: Double Series and Fubini
scenes.summary: Sum the grid by rows first or by columns first — with absolute convergence the answer is the same. \sum_{m,n} \frac{1}{m^2n^2} = \left(\frac{\pi^2}{6}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi^4}{36}. Conditional convergence lets the order change the answer.

scenes.title: Power Series and Radius of Convergence
scenes.summary: A power series \sum a_n x^n converges absolutely inside its radius R and diverges outside — watch three archetypal series pin down their radii, and see why the boundary \lvert x\rvert = R must be decided case by case.

scenes.title: Hadamard Gap Theorem
scenes.summary: S_N(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} z^{2^k} (gap ratio exactly 2): plotting |S_N(r e^{i\theta})| for r \in \{0.90, 0.95, 0.99\}, spikes erupt at more and more angles as N grows — a gappy series with radius exactly 1 is singular at every point of the unit circle. The gap-free contrast \sum z^k/(k+1)^2 stays calm.

scenes.title: Abel's Theorem
scenes.summary: For a convergent series \sum a_n \to S, the power series \sum a_n x^n approaches S as x \to 1^{-} — Abel's theorem. Even the divergent Grandi series points to \frac{1}{2} in this limit, but that is the Abel sum, never "the sum" of the series.

scenes.title: Tauber's Theorem
scenes.summary: Grandi's series has Abel sum \frac{1}{2} yet diverges — because |n\,a_n| = n breaks the hypothesis a_n = o(1/n). The series d_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{(n+1)\ln(n+2)} satisfies it, and its Abel-sum curve reaches the ordinary sum — Tauber's theorem.

scenes.title: Two Roads to e
scenes.summary: Compare how fast compound growth (1+\frac{1}{n})^n and the series \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!} approach e. The factorial series wins by a landslide.

scenes.title: ζ(4) and Even Powers
scenes.summary: The partial sums of \frac{1}{n^4} reach \frac{\pi^4}{90} quickly — and at every even power, the \zeta value closes into a power of \pi.

scenes.title: Rearranging Changes the Sum
scenes.summary: Reordering a conditionally convergent series changes its sum — \ln 2 \approx 0.6931 becomes \frac{3}{2}\ln 2 \approx 1.0397. Twin of the Leibniz scene.

scenes.title: Absolute Convergence
scenes.summary: If the absolute-value series converges, so does the original — compare the two partial-sum walks S_n and T_n settling together against the harmonic-like case where the signs rescue a divergent absolute series.

scenes.title: Riemann's Rearrangement Theorem
scenes.summary: A conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to sum to any real number — watch the greedy block rule steer the alternating harmonic series (which sums to \ln 2 in its natural order) onto a target of your choice.

scenes.title: The Cauchy Product
scenes.summary: (\sum a_n)(\sum b_n) = \sum c_n with c_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k} — sweeping the lattice along diagonals. Mertens' theorem (absolute convergence on one side saves the product) and the counterexample when both converge only conditionally.

scenes.title: The Weierstrass M-Test
scenes.summary: If a majorant M_n dominates every term at all x and \sum M_n converges, the series converges uniformly — here \left|\frac{\sin(nx)}{n^2}\right| \le \frac{1}{n^2} =: M_n and \sum M_n = \frac{\pi^2}{6}, so the partial-sum error band tightens across the whole x-interval at once.

scenes.title: Dini's Theorem
scenes.summary: On a compact set, a monotone sequence of continuous functions converging pointwise converges uniformly — a finite subcover of the open sets E_n grabs them all at once. The twin tool of the M-test.

scenes.title: The Ringing That Never Dies
scenes.summary: Layer sine waves onto a square wave. The ringing beside each jump never dies out, no matter how large N gets.

scenes.title: Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma
scenes.summary: Fourier coefficients die out — \int f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx \to 0. Rapid oscillation averages away every bump of f.

scenes.title: Fejér's Theorem
scenes.summary: The Cesàro means \sigma_N of Fourier partial sums converge uniformly for continuous functions — because the Fejér kernel is an approximate identity. Overlay the ringing S_N with the smooth \sigma_N.

scenes.title: Parseval's Identity
scenes.summary: Energy is conserved — \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |f|^2 = \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum (a_n^2 + b_n^2). Watch the fraction of energy captured by the first N modes.

scenes.title: The Gibbs Phenomenon
scenes.summary: Why the bump beside the jump never dies — rescaling by t = 2Nx collapses S_N onto (2/\pi)\mathrm{Si}(t), and the first peak tends to (2/\pi)\mathrm{Si}(\pi) \approx 1.179. The overshoot is about 8.95% of the jump.

scenes.title: Differentiable Implies Continuous
scenes.summary: Differentiable implies continuous, but not conversely — zoom into the corner of |x| and it never flattens. The first step of the differentiation scenes.

scenes.title: A Discontinuous Derivative
scenes.summary: f(x) = x^2\sin(1/x) (f(0) = 0) is differentiable everywhere with f'(0) = 0, yet the derivative f'(x) = 2x\sin(1/x) - \cos(1/x) oscillates and is discontinuous at 0. Differentiable does not imply continuously differentiable — though derivatives still keep the intermediate value property (Darboux).

scenes.title: The Secant Meets Its Parallel Tangent
scenes.summary: Somewhere on the curve, a tangent is parallel to the secant of slope \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}. Drag \xi to find it.

scenes.title: Derivative Sign and Monotonicity
scenes.summary: The sign of f' decides where the curve rises and falls: up on the green background (f' > 0), down on the red one (f' < 0). Drag x_0 and watch the tangent's color track the sign — one step behind the Mean Value Theorem.

scenes.title: The Inverse Function Theorem
scenes.summary: If f'(a) \ne 0, f can be flipped near a, and the flipped function's slope is the reciprocal — the two tangent slopes multiply to exactly 1.

scenes.title: Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem
scenes.summary: On the parametric curve (g(t), f(t)) a tangent parallel to the chord exists. For f(t) = t^2, g(t) = t^3 it sits at \xi = 14/9.

scenes.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
scenes.summary: In a 0/0 or \infty/\infty form, differentiating the numerator and the denominator keeps the limit. Drive x toward the limit point and watch \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} track \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}.

scenes.title: Darboux's Theorem
scenes.summary: Derivatives have the intermediate value property even when discontinuous — f'(x) = 2x\sin(1/x) - \cos(1/x) oscillates wildly near 0 yet steps on every level. Jump discontinuities are impossible in a derivative.

scenes.title: The Weierstrass Function
scenes.summary: W(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^n\cos(b^n\pi x) — continuous everywhere yet differentiable nowhere. The M-test scene powers the continuity argument, and the graph turns thornier as partial sums grow. The full nowhere-differentiability proof is idea-level only.

scenes.title: Polynomials Hugging the Curve
scenes.summary: Lay the Maclaurin polynomial T_n(x) over \sin x. Raise the degree and watch it hug the curve.

scenes.title: Taylor's Theorem: The Remainder Envelope
scenes.summary: The error R_n(x) is trapped in the band T_n(x) \pm |x|^{n+1}/(n+1)!. Raise n and the band shrinks to zero.

scenes.title: Convex Functions
scenes.summary: Convex when the chord floats above the graph — for differentiable f this is the same as f' increasing, and the second derivative decides it. Up to Jensen's inequality.

scenes.title: Riding Tangents to the Root
scenes.summary: Ride the tangent down to the root. The number of correct digits doubles each step.

scenes.title: The Contraction Cobweb
scenes.summary: The cobweb between y = x and y = f(x) gets sucked into one point. The error shrinks like q^n.

scenes.title: The Gamma Function
scenes.summary: The factorial stretched to real arguments — \Gamma(x+1) = x\Gamma(x), so \Gamma(n+1) = n!. Watch the improper integral converge for x > 0.

scenes.title: The Beta Function
scenes.summary: The area under \t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\ is the beta function — morph its shape with the \p\, \q\ sliders. Also covers \B(p,q) = \\Gamma(p)\\Gamma(q)/\\Gamma(p+q)\, the bridge to the gamma function.

scenes.title: Bohr–Mollerup Theorem
scenes.summary: f(1) = 1 and f(x+1) = x\,f(x) do not pin down the continuous extension of the factorial — the impostor \Gamma(x)(1 + a\sin 2\pi x) matches \Gamma at every integer and survives. Watch the secant test expose log-convexity as \Gamma's true fingerprint.

scenes.title: Improper Integrals
scenes.summary: \int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^p} converges only for p > 1, plus the singular kind \int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = 2 — the twin of the p-series scene.

scenes.title: Gabriel's Horn
scenes.summary: Rotating y = 1/x (x \ge 1) makes a horn with finite volume \pi but infinite surface area — fillable with \pi of paint, yet unpaintable. The painter's paradox.

scenes.title: Upper and Lower Sums Close In
scenes.summary: Fill rectangles under f(x) = x^2. The lower and upper sums squeeze \frac{1}{3} from both sides.

scenes.title: The Dirichlet Function
scenes.summary: \mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{Q}} is 1 on the rationals and 0 on the irrationals of [0, 1] — every subinterval holds both, so the upper sum is always 1 and the lower sum always 0. The canonical non-Riemann-integrable function: no refinement closes the gap.

scenes.title: Volterra's Function
scenes.summary: Differentiable everywhere with a bounded derivative — yet the derivative is not Riemann integrable. A sum of (x-a)^2(b-x)^2\sin\frac{1}{x-a}-type bumps over a fat Cantor set builds this legendary counterexample.

scenes.title: The Area Function's Derivative Is the Function
scenes.summary: Measure the slope of the area function A(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt — it equals f(x). Drag x.

scenes.title: Integration by Parts
scenes.summary: Integrate the product rule and get \int u\,dv = [uv] - \int v\,du — split the area into two pieces and compute each. Move b: both sides agree to the last decimal.

scenes.title: Change of Variables
scenes.summary: Stretch and squeeze the axis with u = \varphi(x) and the limits follow — \int_a^b f(\varphi)\varphi' = \int_{\varphi(a)}^{\varphi(b)} f. Watch two substitutions collapse onto the same integral.

scenes.title: Functions of Bounded Variation
scenes.summary: A function has bounded variation when \sum \lvert f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})\rvert stays under a finite ceiling as partitions refine — every monotone function qualifies, while x\sin(1/x), wiggling endlessly near 0, does not.

scenes.title: The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
scenes.summary: Changing the integrator — \int_a^b f\,d\alpha weighs intervals by \Delta\alpha_i = \alpha(x_i) - \alpha(x_{i-1}) instead of length. \alpha(x) = x recovers Riemann sums, a step \alpha collapses to a single jump, \alpha(x) = x^2 gives \int f\alpha'\,dx.

scenes.title: Jordan Decomposition
scenes.summary: Every BV function is a difference of two increasing functions — f = g - h with g(x) = V_0^x(f) the variation function. Drag the probe point over x^2\sin\frac{1}{x} and watch the identity hold pointwise.

scenes.title: Lebesgue Measure
scenes.summary: Outer measure is the cheapest countable interval cover of a set. A single point — and even all the rationals — cost nothing. Measurable sets and countable additivity need the Carathéodory construction (idea level only).

scenes.title: The Vitali Set
scenes.summary: Using the axiom of choice to pick one representative from each class of \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Q} births a non-measurable set. Countably many disjoint translates cover [0,1] inside [-1,2] — yet measure 0 gives total 0 and positive measure gives infinity. Both impossible.

scenes.title: Borel–Cantelli Lemmas
scenes.summary: If the total length is finite, the points hit infinitely often form a null set — \sum m(E_n) < \infty \Rightarrow m(\limsup E_n) = 0. With independence the converse holds.

scenes.title: Covering the Rationals with Nothing
scenes.summary: Cover the rationals one by one with \varepsilon/2^k covers — the total length drops below \varepsilon. Riemann can't move.

scenes.title: Lebesgue Convergence Theorems
scenes.summary: Monotone convergence, Fatou, dominated convergence — the three pillars for swapping limits and integrals. Watch mass escape (escape·spike) to see why each hypothesis is needed.

scenes.title: Fubini–Tonelli Theorem
scenes.summary: Nonnegative (Tonelli) or integrable (Fubini) functions give the same iterated integrals in either order — rows-first or columns-first. Without integrability it breaks.

scenes.title: Egorov's Theorem
scenes.summary: On finite measure, a.e. convergence is "almost" uniform — squeeze the bad set's measure below \varepsilon and convergence is uniform on the rest.

scenes.title: Absolute Continuity
scenes.summary: F(x) = x^2 is absolutely continuous — when the intervals' total length goes to 0, so does \sum |\Delta F|. The Cantor function is uniformly continuous but not absolutely continuous: total length \left(\frac23\right)^n \to 0 while \sum |\Delta c| = 1 stays frozen. Absolutely continuous functions are exactly the indefinite integrals of Lebesgue-integrable functions.

scenes.title: Differentiation Under the Integral Sign
scenes.summary: F(x) = \int_0^1 t^x\,dt = \frac{1}{x+1} — drag along the curve and its tangent while the numerics confirm that differentiating inside the integral, \int_0^1 t^x \ln t\,dt, gives the tangent slope -\frac{1}{(x+1)^2}.

scenes.title: Minkowski's Inequality
scenes.summary: The L^p triangle inequality — \|f+g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p on [0,1]. With f(t) = t^a, g(t) = (1-t)^b, sliding p opens and closes the gap between the two bars. At p = 1 linearity of the integral closes the gap to 0.

terms.definition: A statement that is either true or false — proof is the art of combining propositions with connectives and tracking how the truth values are forced.
A proof that takes the hypothesis as given and reaches the conclusion by a straight chain of justified steps — no detours.
Splitting the domain into cases that cover everything, and proving the claim in each case — together the cases cover the whole proof.
terms.sceneTitle: Proof by Cases and Existence Proofs

terms.definition: g \circ f — apply f first, then g to the result. Injectivity and surjectivity propagate through composition in provable ways.
\forall (for all) and \exists (there exists) — the symbols that pin down precisely how a statement ranges over its domain. Negation swaps the two.
The contrapositive of P \Rightarrow Q is \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P — always equivalent to the original, so it can be proved in its place when the direct route stalls.
The method that assumes the negation of the conclusion and derives a contradiction — if assuming \lnot P yields a contradiction (\bot), then P holds.
P \iff Q — an "if and only if" claim that is completed only by proving the two directions P \Rightarrow Q and Q \Rightarrow P separately.
terms.sceneTitle: Counterexamples and If and Only If

terms.definition: Induction that assumes all of P(2), \dots, P(n-1) when proving P(n) — used when the step needs much smaller values, like the factors of n.
A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive — its equivalence classes partition the whole set without overlap.
1, 2, 3, \dots — the basic unit of counting, axiomatized by Peano.
The proof principle getting P(n) for every natural n from P(1) and P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1) — like dominoes falling in turn.
The five axioms defining the naturals — existence of 1, the successor function, the induction axiom, and more. Addition and multiplication are defined recursively from them.
\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} — the number of ways to choose k from n. Satisfies Pascal's identity \binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}=\binom{n+1}{k}.
(x+y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^{n-k}y^k — proved by induction, with Pascal's identity as the inductive step.
\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots — built as equivalence classes of natural pairs with (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c (the number "a-b").
\frac{a}{b} (b \ne 0) — built as equivalence classes of integer pairs with (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff ad=bc; they form a field.
The set of elements equivalent under an equivalence relation — the key technique for "building" the integers, rationals, and reals.
A collection of distinct objects. Every discussion in analysis begins with a set.
A rule assigning to each element of a domain exactly one element of a codomain.
The least of the upper bounds of a set, written \sup A.
The greatest of the lower bounds of a set, written \inf A.
The x \ge 0 with x^n = a; its existence is guaranteed by \sup\{x \ge 0 : x^n < a\}.
The axiom that a choice function exists for any collection of nonempty sets.
If every chain has an upper bound, a maximal element exists. Equivalent to the axiom of choice.
Every set is smaller than its power set: |X| < |\mathcal{P}(X)|, proved by diagonalization.
A set that can be put in one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers; the rationals are the classic example.
A set with one associative operation, an identity element, and inverses.
A set forming a group under each of addition and multiplication, with distributivity; the rationals and the reals are examples.
A set closed under addition and scalar multiplication; \mathbb{R}^n is the prototype.
A structure-preserving bijection. Isomorphic spaces are "the same structure in different packaging".
The number of elements in a basis of a vector space.
The dimension of the image of a linear map.
x_n \to L when for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N with |x_n - L| < \varepsilon for all n > N.
The "length" \|x\| of a vector; the metric is d(x,y) = \|x - y\|.
The space of sequences with finite p-th power sum; \ell^1 \subset \ell^2 \subset \ell^\infty.
|\langle x,y\rangle| \le \|x\|\,\|y\| — the inner product never exceeds the product of the norms; equality holds exactly for parallel vectors.
A real number that is not rational; \sqrt{2} is the classic example.
An equivalence class of Cauchy sequences of rationals — the rationals with their gaps filled.
A sequence whose terms get arbitrarily close to each other; equivalent to convergence in \mathbb{R}.
Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.
terms.sceneTitle: A Convergent Subsequence Always Hides Inside

terms.definition: A sequence that is always increasing or always decreasing; if bounded, it converges.
The value the tail suprema \\\sup_{n \\ge N} a_n\ settle to as \N \\to \\infty\ — the largest cluster point of the sequence.
The value the tail infima \\\inf_{n \\ge N} a_n\ settle to as \N \\to \\infty\ — the smallest cluster point of the sequence.
The sequence l'Hôpital: if (b_n) is strictly increasing and unbounded and the difference ratio \frac{a_{n+1}-a_n}{b_{n+1}-b_n} tends to L, so does \frac{a_n}{b_n}.
The rigorous definition of a function limit: for every error \varepsilon there is a tolerance \delta.
f(x) \to f(a) as x \to a; the graph has no breaks.
Every discontinuity of a monotone function is a jump; only finitely many jumps exceed 1/n, so the discontinuities are at most countable.
Continuity with a single \delta working across the whole domain; 1/x is continuous but not uniformly continuous on (0,1].
A continuous function takes every value between any two of its values.
terms.sceneTitle: You Can't Climb Without Crossing Every Height

terms.definition: A continuous function on a closed interval attains a maximum and a minimum.
Convergence of a sequence of functions with one N working for all x; it preserves continuity of the limit.
Convergence at each point separately; the limit may be discontinuous.
A set in which every point is an interior point; it contains none of its boundary.
A set whose complement is open; it contains all its limit points.
A set together with all its limit points, written \overline{A}.
A set that fits inside some interval (or ball).
A closed and bounded set (Heine–Borel in \mathbb{R}); every sequence has a subsequence converging inside the set.
A set of reals is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
A set equipped with a distance d(x,y) between points.
A distance function satisfying symmetry, non-negativity, and the triangle inequality.
A metric space where every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.
A point with Tx = x; a contraction on a complete metric space has a unique one.
A countable union of nowhere dense sets — by the Baire Category Theorem, a complete metric space cannot be meagre in itself.
A topological space in which every countable intersection of dense open sets is dense — complete metric spaces and locally compact Hausdorff spaces are the key examples.
A function expressible as the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous functions — Thomae's function is the poster child; its continuity points always contain a dense G_\delta.
At x, \omega_f(x) = \inf\{\mathrm{diam}\,f(U) : U \text{ a neighborhood of } x\} measures local spread; \omega_f(x) = 0 iff f is continuous at x.
The set left after repeatedly removing middle thirds; it has length zero yet is uncountable.
A Cantor-type set built by removing only length 4^{-n} at each stage — compact, nowhere dense and perfect, yet keeping measure \frac12. Also called the Smith–Volterra–Cantor set.
The continuous nondecreasing function that climbs only on the Cantor set — constant on every complementary interval, so f'=0 on a set of total length 1.
Nickname for the Cantor function — infinitely many flat steps, yet it climbs from 0 to 1.
The class of functions for which the FTC holds — guaranteeing f(b)-f(a) = \int_a^b f'. The Cantor function is continuous but not absolutely continuous.
A set that is both open and closed. In \mathbb{R} only \varnothing and \mathbb{R} qualify, but subspaces admit nontrivial examples.
The closure of \{(x, \sin(1/x)) : x > 0\} — the canonical example of a connected but not path-connected curve.
A continuous surjection [0,1] \to [0,1]^2 — a space-filling curve. Injectivity is impossible.

A family \mathcal{F} of functions that is continuous with "the same \delta" at every point — for each \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 working for all f \in \mathcal{F}. The key hypothesis of the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem.
A set whose closure is compact — every sequence hides a convergent subsequence. In C(K) this is equivalent to uniform boundedness + equicontinuity (Arzelà–Ascoli).
Every continuous function on a closed interval can be uniformly approximated by polynomials.
B_n(f)(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} f(k/n)\binom{n}{k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k}; used in the constructive proof of the approximation theorem.
The property that for any two distinct points x \ne y there is a function u in the algebra \mathcal{A} with u(x) \ne u(y). One of the key hypotheses of the Stone–Weierstrass theorem.

A set of functions closed under linear combinations and products. Trigonometric polynomials form a subalgebra via product-to-sum identities (e.g. \cos A \cos B = \tfrac12(\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B))), and by the Stone–Weierstrass theorem it is uniformly dense in C(S^1).
For 0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \cdots, \operatorname{span}\{1, x^{\lambda_1}, x^{\lambda_2}, \ldots\} is dense in C[0,1] if and only if \sum \frac{1}{\lambda_n} = \infty.
\sum 1/n: its terms tend to 0, yet the sum diverges.
A series whose partial sums have no finite limit.
\gamma = \lim_{n\to\infty}(H_n - \ln n) \approx 0.5772 — the value the gap between harmonic numbers and the logarithm settles at.
H_n = 1 + \frac12 + \cdots + \frac1n — the partial sums of the harmonic series.
The problem of showing \sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6.
For s > 1, \zeta(s) = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1} — sieving out composite terms leaves only the product over primes.
A series with alternating signs; it converges if its terms decrease monotonically to 0 (Leibniz test).
Deciding convergence by comparing terms against a reference series.
Deciding convergence from the limit of |a_{n+1}/a_n|.
For a decreasing positive function, the series and the improper integral converge or diverge together.
A series with terms on the grid ((m,n)); with absolute convergence, rows-first and columns-first sums agree.
L = \lim n(a_n/a_{n+1} - 1): converges if L > 1, diverges if L < 1. The test to reach for when the ratio drifts to 1 and the ratio test goes silent.
With K_n = p_n a_n/a_{n+1} - p_{n+1}: convergence if K_n stays positive, divergence if K_n \le 0 and \sum 1/p_n diverges. p_n = 1 gives the ratio test, p_n = n gives Raabe's.
If a_n/a_{n+1} = 1 + h/n + O(1/n^r) (r > 1): converges for h > 1, diverges for h < 1 — a corollary of Kummer's test.
For decreasing a_n \ge 0, \sum a_n and \sum 2^n a_{2^n} share convergence.
A series whose neighboring terms cancel, leaving a simple partial sum.
\sum ar^n; converges to a/(1-r) when |r| < 1.
An infinite product representation of \pi/2.
The asymptotic n! \approx \sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n.
n! = 1\cdot 2\cdots n.
1-1+1-1+\cdots; divergent in the usual sense.
The limit of the averaged partial sums; the Grandi series sums to 1/2 this way.
If the partial sums of \(a_n)\ are bounded and \(b_n)\ decreases to 0, then \\\sum a_n b_n\ converges.
If \sum a_n converges and (b_n) is monotone and bounded, then \sum a_n b_n converges. Unlike Dirichlet's test, (b_n) need not tend to 0.
\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k b_k = A_n b_{n+1} - A_{m-1} b_m + \sum_{k=m}^{n} A_k (b_k - b_{k+1}) — the discrete integration by parts; the engine behind Abel's test.
A series of the form \sum a_n(x-c)^n.
terms.sceneTitle: Power Series and Radius of Convergence

terms.definition: The radius of the interval on which a power series converges.
terms.sceneTitle: Power Series and Radius of Convergence

terms.definition: A sparse layout of exponents in \sum a_k z^{n_k} with n_{k+1}/n_k \ge q > 1 — e.g. n_k = 2^k (ratio exactly 2). With radius 1, the whole unit circle becomes a natural boundary.
A curve past no point of which a holomorphic function can be analytically continued — for \sum z^{2^k} the unit circle |z| = 1 is exactly that, by the Hadamard gap theorem.
If \sum a_n \to S then \lim_{x\to 1^{-}}\sum a_n x^n = S — the boundary value of the power series recovers the ordinary sum.
The value of \lim_{x\to 1^{-}}\sum a_n x^n when it exists. Assigns values to divergent series, but is never "the sum" — the Abel sum of Grandi's series is 1/2.
A theorem recovering ordinary convergence from a weaker summability method (like Abel summation) under an extra condition on the terms, e.g. a_n = o(1/n) — Tauber's theorem is the prototype.
The base of the natural logarithm: \lim (1+1/n)^n = \sum 1/n!.
\zeta(s) = \sum 1/n^s; the Basel problem is \zeta(2) = \pi^2/6.
Absolutely convergent series keep their sum under reordering; conditionally convergent ones need not.
Convergence without absolute convergence.
Convergence of \sum |a_n|; it implies convergence.
A conditionally convergent real series can be rearranged to converge to any real number (or \pm\infty) — because its positive and negative parts each diverge.
The product of two series (\sum a_n)(\sum b_n) = \sum c_n with c_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k} — diagonal sums.
If one series converges absolutely and the other converges, their Cauchy product converges to the product of the sums.
If \|f_n(x)| \\le M_n\ for all \x\ and \\\sum M_n\ converges, then \\\sum f_n\ converges uniformly.
On a compact set, a monotone sequence of continuous functions converging pointwise to a continuous limit converges uniformly.
A periodic function expressed as a sine-cosine series.
K_N(t) = \frac1N\left(\frac{\sin(Nt/2)}{\sin(t/2)}\right)^2 — a nonnegative trigonometric polynomial of mean 1 that turns Cesàro means of Fourier sums into a convolution.
The average of partial sums \sigma_N = \frac{S_0+\cdots+S_{N-1}}{N} — it can sum divergent series, and for Fourier series it smooths out the ringing (Fejér's theorem).
Fourier partial sums overshoot by about 8.95% of the jump near a discontinuity — raising N narrows the bump but never removes it.
The limiting Gibbs overshoot \frac{2}{\pi}\mathrm{Si}(\pi) - 1 \approx 0.17898 — about 8.949% of the jump. \mathrm{Si} is the sine integral.
Having a tangent line at the point; differentiability implies continuity.
If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), some c satisfies f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a).
terms.sceneTitle: The Secant Meets Its Parallel Tangent

terms.definition: If f'(a) \ne 0, f has a local inverse near a with (f^{-1})'(f(a)) = 1/f'(a).
The mean value theorem for two functions; the basis of l'Hôpital's rule.
A 0/0 or \infty/\infty limit equals the limit of the differentiated numerator over denominator.
A derivative has the intermediate value property even when discontinuous — if f'(a) < c < f'(b) then some \xi \in (a,b) has f'(\xi) = c.
The intermediate value property without continuity — derivatives are the canonical examples.
An interior local max/min where f is differentiable forces f'(c) = 0. Used to prove Darboux's theorem.
0 for x < 0, 1 for x \ge 0. Its jump discontinuity means it can never be anyone's derivative.
Left and right limits both exist but differ. Impossible in a derivative.
Continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere — \sum a^n\cos(b^n\pi x). Shows a uniform limit of smooth functions need not be differentiable.
The power series built from a function's derivatives at x=a.
The theorem giving the Taylor polynomial together with the exact form of the remainder R_n.
A function whose chords lie above its graph: f(tx+(1-t)y) \le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y).
For convex f: f of the average \le the average of f.
The iteration x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) for finding roots.
A contraction on a complete metric space has a unique fixed point.
A map that shrinks distances by a fixed ratio below 1.
\Gamma(x) = \int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt; the continuous extension of the factorial (\Gamma(n+1) = n!).
B(p,q) = \int_0^1 t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt (p, q > 0). Linked to the gamma function by B(p,q) = \Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)/\Gamma(p+q).
The property that \ln f is convex. Together with f(1) = 1 and f(x+1) = x\,f(x), it characterizes \Gamma uniquely (Bohr–Mollerup theorem).
An integral over an unbounded interval or of an unbounded function, defined as a limit.
The limit of Riemann sums over finer and finer partitions.
terms.sceneTitle: Upper and Lower Sums Close In

terms.definition: The set of cut points dividing an interval.
terms.sceneTitle: Upper and Lower Sums Close In

terms.definition: Differentiable everywhere with a bounded derivative, yet the derivative is not Riemann integrable — built by stacking (x-a)^2(b-x)^2\sin\frac{1}{x-a}-type bumps over a fat Cantor set.
Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
terms.sceneTitle: The Area Function's Derivative Is the Function

terms.definition: \int u\,dv = [uv] - \int v\,du: the product rule, integrated.
With u = \varphi(x), \int_a^b f(\varphi)\varphi' = \int_{\varphi(a)}^{\varphi(b)} f: the limits follow the substitution.
The sum \sum \lvert f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})\rvert stays under a finite ceiling as partitions refine. Every monotone function has bounded variation.
A function of bounded variation is the difference of two increasing functions: f = g - h.
Writing a BV function f as the difference f = g - h of two increasing functions g, h — always possible with g(x) = V_a^x(f) (the variation function) and h = g - f.
g(x) = V_a^x(f): the total variation of f over [a, x]. For a BV f it is increasing, and h = g - f is increasing too — giving the Jordan decomposition f = g - h.
The extension of length, area, and volume to sets.
A set coverable by intervals of arbitrarily small total length.
Integration by slicing the range of values; applies to a wider class of functions than the Riemann integral.

The property that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 with \sum |F(b_i) - F(a_i)| < \varepsilon whenever \sum (b_i - a_i) < \delta — the "absolute" strengthening of uniform continuity. Exactly the indefinite integrals of L^1 functions.
No rational p/q satisfies (p/q)^2 = 2 — proved by infinite descent on lowest terms, exposing a "hole" in the rational line.
Between any reals x < y lies a rational — take n > 1/(y-x) and m = \lfloor nx \rfloor + 1, then x < m/n < y.
If |x| < 1 then x^n \to 0; if x > 1 then x^{1/n} \to 1 — the basic fates of powers and roots.
The \varepsilon-\delta definition, sequential preservation, and open preimages of open sets — three lenses on the same continuity.
f' \ge 0 makes f increasing, f' > 0 strictly increasing (by MVT) — the sign of the derivative decides rise and fall.
1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals — every upper sum is 1 and every lower sum 0, so it is not Riemann integrable.
\int_a^b f\,d\alpha = \lim \sum f(\xi_i)\,\Delta\alpha_i — reduces to the Riemann integral for \alpha(x) = x; a jump lets one point's value dominate.
Monotone convergence, Fatou, dominated convergence — three conditions for \int \lim f_n = \lim \int f_n. Escaping mass breaks them.
For nonnegative (Tonelli) or integrable (Fubini) functions, iterated integrals agree in either order.
On finite measure, a.e. convergence is uniform after removing a set of arbitrarily small measure.
If \sum m(E_n) < \infty, the limsup set has measure 0; with independence the converse holds.
Fourier coefficients of an integrable function tend to 0 — rapid oscillation averages every bump away.
\frac1\pi\int |f|^2 = \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum(a_n^2+b_n^2) — conservation of energy.
\sum|a_kb_k| \le \|a\|_p\|b\|_q (\frac1p+\frac1q=1) — Cauchy–Schwarz is p=q=2.
f(p/q) = 1/q (reduced), f(x) = 0 (irrational) — the popcorn function, continuous at every irrational and discontinuous at every rational.
x^2\sin(1/x) is differentiable everywhere, yet its derivative is discontinuous at 0 — differentiable does not imply continuously differentiable.
The solid of revolution of y = 1/x (x \ge 1) — finite volume \pi, infinite surface area. The painter's paradox.
A choice-set of representatives of \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Q} via the axiom of choice — not Lebesgue measurable.
\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^b f(x,t)\,dt = \int_a^b \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,t)\,dt — holds when \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} is continuous. Also called Leibniz's rule.
The L^p triangle inequality \|f+g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p (p \ge 1) — derived from Hölder's inequality.

exercises.statement: Write the full negation of the statement \forall x \in \mathbb{R}\ \exists y \in \mathbb{R}\ (y^2 > x) (flip one quantifier at a time). Then prove which of the statement and its negation is true.
Prove by direct proof that the product of two odd integers is odd.
Prove by contrapositive that if 5n + 4 is even then n is even. Also explain why a direct proof (starting from the assumption that 5n+4 is even) is awkward.
Prove by contradiction that there is no smallest positive real number.

Prove by strong induction that every integer amount n \ge 8 can be formed with 3-unit and 5-unit stamps — i.e. there exist integers a, b \ge 0 with n = 3a + 5b. Explain why three base cases are needed.

Prove that the relation (a, b) \sim (c, d) \iff a^2 + b^2 = c^2 + d^2 on \mathbb{R}^2 is an equivalence relation, and show that each equivalence class is a circle centered at the origin (the class of the origin being the single point itself).

Let a_n = \frac{n + \sin n}{n^2 + 1}. Prove directly from the \varepsilon-N definition that \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0, and give an explicit formula for a usable N(\varepsilon) in terms of \varepsilon > 0.

For n \ge 1 let a_n = \frac{\lfloor n\sqrt{2} \rfloor}{n}, where \lfloor x \rfloor is the greatest integer \le x. (a) Show each a_n is rational. (b) Prove a_n \to \sqrt{2} from the \varepsilon-N definition. (c) Prove \sqrt{2} is irrational. Conclude that a sequence of rationals can converge to an irrational limit.
Let a_n = (2 + (-1)^n)\left(1 - \frac{1}{n+1}\right). Find \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n and \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n, with a rigorous proof using subsequence arguments.
Let a_n > 0 with a_n \to L > 0. Prove the geometric mean G_n = (a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n)^{1/n} converges to L. (Hint: taking logarithms turns this into a Cesaro mean.)

For a sequence with a_n > 0, prove \liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} a_n^{1/n} \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n^{1/n} \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}. Additionally, if \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \to L > 0, take logarithms and use the Stolz-Cesaro theorem to show a_n^{1/n} \to L.
True or false, with proof: the continuous image of an open interval is always an open set.

On \mathbb{R} let f_n(x) = \frac{x}{1 + n x^2}. Find the pointwise limit \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) at each x, prove the convergence is uniform on \mathbb{R}, and compute the exact value of \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f_n(x)|.

An irrational x is a Liouville number if for every m \ge 1 there are infinitely many integer pairs (p, q) with q \ge 2 satisfying |x - p/q| < 1/q^m. For k \ge 1 put U_k = \bigcup_{q \ge 2}\bigcup_{p \in \mathbb{Z}} (p/q - 1/q^k,\ p/q + 1/q^k). (a) Show each U_k is a dense open set in \mathbb{R}. (b) Show G = \bigcap_{k \ge 1} U_k \cap \bigcap_{j \ge 1} (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{r_j\}), where \{r_j\} enumerates the rationals, is a G_\delta set all of whose elements are Liouville numbers. (c) Use the Baire category theorem to conclude the Liouville numbers are dense in \mathbb{R} and uncountable.

Let T(x) = \frac{\cos x + 1}{4} for x \in [0, 1]. (a) Show T maps [0, 1] into itself and is a contraction (name the contraction constant). (b) Conclude T has a unique fixed point x^* \in [0, 1]. (c) With x_0 = 0 and x_{n+1} = T(x_n), use the error bound |x_n - x^*| \le \frac{q^n}{1-q}|x_1 - x_0| to find the smallest n guaranteeing |x_n - x^*| < 10^{-3}.
Let C be the set of points in [0, 1] possessing a ternary expansion using only the digits 0 and 2 (the standard middle-thirds Cantor set). For C + C = \{x + y : x, y \in C\}, prove C + C = [0, 2].

Let C(f) be the set of points where f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} is continuous. (a) Using the oscillation \omega_f(x) = \inf_{\delta > 0} \sup\{|f(y) - f(z)| : y, z \in (x-\delta, x+\delta)\}, show C(f) = \bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty} \{x : \omega_f(x) < 1/k\} with each \{x : \omega_f(x) < 1/k\} open; i.e. C(f) is a G_\delta set. (b) Use the Baire category theorem to show \mathbb{Q} is not a G_\delta subset of \mathbb{R}. (c) Conclude no function f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} is continuous exactly at the rationals and discontinuous exactly at the irrationals.
Let f be continuous on [0, 1] and suppose \int_0^1 x^n f(x)\,dx = 0 for every integer n \ge 0. Use the Weierstrass approximation theorem to prove f \equiv 0.
Prove that \sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{\ln n}{n^2} converges, using the limit comparison test.
For N \ge 2, evaluate the partial product P_N = \prod_{n=2}^{N}\left(1-\frac{1}{n^2}\right) and prove \lim_{N\to\infty} P_N = \frac{1}{2}.
Show that \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n(n+1)} converges, compute the third partial sum S_3, and bound the remainder |S - S_3|.
Explain why the ratio test is inconclusive for \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(2n)!}{4^n (n!)^2}\cdot\frac{1}{n}, then prove convergence with Raabe's test.
Prove that \sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{\,n+(-1)^n\sqrt{n}\,} converges conditionally. (Hint: use \frac{1}{1+u} = 1-u+\frac{u^2}{1+u}.)
For real p, prove by applying the condensation test twice that the Bertrand series \sum_{n=3}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n\,\ln n\,(\ln\ln n)^p} converges if and only if p > 1.

Using the Euler product, prove that the infinite product \prod_{p\ \text{prime}}\left(1+\frac{1}{p^2}\right) converges and equals \frac{15}{\pi^2}. (You may use \zeta(2) = \frac{\pi^2}{6} and \zeta(4) = \frac{\pi^4}{90} as known.)
Find the radius of convergence of the power series \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{n^2+1}{3^n}\,x^n.
Prove that \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n(-1)^n diverges in the ordinary sense but is Abel summable, with Abel sum -\frac{1}{4}.

Prove rigorously that the rearrangement of the alternating harmonic series taking "two positive terms, then one negative term" in order, 1+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{7}-\frac{1}{4}+\cdots, converges to \frac{3}{2}\ln 2. (You may use H_m = \ln m+\gamma+o(1) as known.)
Show that \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2+x^2} converges uniformly on all of \mathbb{R} by the M-test, and prove its sum is continuous on \mathbb{R}.
Let s_N(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{N}(1-x)x^n for N \ge 1. (a) Show s_N converges uniformly on [0,a] (0 < a < 1) via Dini's theorem. (b) Prove it does not converge uniformly on [0,1].

Let K_n \ge 0 be continuous 2\pi-periodic kernels satisfying: (i) \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} K_n(t)\,dt = 1; (ii) mass concentration: for every \delta > 0, \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\delta \le \lvert t \rvert \le \pi} K_n(t)\,dt \to 0 as n \to \infty. For f continuous and 2\pi-periodic, prove the convolution (f \ast K_n)(x) = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x-t)K_n(t)\,dt converges to f uniformly. (The Fejér kernel satisfies these hypotheses — see the Fejér scene — so this generalizes Fejér's theorem.)

Let f be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with \lvert f'(x) \rvert \le M for all x \in (a,b) and some constant M \ge 0. Prove that \lvert f(x) - f(y) \rvert \le M\lvert x - y \rvert for all x, y \in [a,b]. (Hence f is uniformly continuous on [a,b].)

Start Newton's iteration for x^2 - 2 = 0, x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{x_n^2 - 2}{2x_n} = \dfrac{x_n + 2/x_n}{2}, at x_0 = 1. (a) Show x_n > 0 for all n. (b) Use AM-GM to show x_{n+1} \ge \sqrt{2} for all n. (c) Show x_1 > \sqrt{2} and that (x_n)_{n \ge 1} is decreasing. (d) Conclude x_n \to \sqrt{2}.

Prove via the triangle inequality that f(x) = \lvert x \rvert is convex on \mathbb{R}, and cite the continuity theorem for convex functions to conclude f is continuous. Show f is not differentiable at 0, confirming that convexity does not imply differentiability.
Let f be differentiable on [a,b] with f'(x) \ne 0 for every x \in [a,b]. Combining Darboux's theorem with the Mean Value Theorem, prove that f is strictly monotone on [a,b].

Let f be n+1 times continuously differentiable on [a,b] (n \ge 0). For a \le x \le b, prove Taylor's formula with integral remainder
      \[f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k + R_n(x), \qquad R_n(x) = \frac{1}{n!}\int_a^x (x-t)^n f^{(n+1)}(t)\,dt.\]
      The case n = 0 is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus; for the induction step apply integration by parts once.

Consider the map T(x) = \dfrac{1}{2+x} on [0,1]. (a) Show T maps [0,1] into itself and is a contraction with constant c = 1/4. (b) Cite the Banach fixed point theorem to find the unique fixed point of T (solve the quadratic), and explain why iteration from any starting point converges to it.

Let f(x) = e^{-1/x^2} for x \ne 0 and f(0) = 0. Prove f is infinitely differentiable on \mathbb{R} with f^{(n)}(0) = 0 for every n \ge 0. Deduce that the Maclaurin series of f converges for every x but equals f(x) only at x = 0 — a Taylor series need not recover the function.
Define f on [0,1] by f(1/2) = 1 and f(x) = 0 for x \ne 1/2. Prove directly from upper and lower sums that f is Riemann integrable with \int_0^1 f = 0.

Let F(x) = x^2\sin(1/x^2) for x \ne 0 and F(0) = 0. Show F is differentiable at every point of [-1,1], but that F' is unbounded on every neighborhood of 0. Conclude F' is not Riemann integrable on [-1,1], and explain why this shows the hypothesis "the derivative is Riemann integrable" in FTC-II cannot be dropped.

Let f and g be of bounded variation on [a,b]. First show a BV function is bounded (hint: \lvert f(x) - f(a) \rvert \le V_a^b(f)), then prove the product fg is also of bounded variation on [a,b]. Find an upper bound for its total variation.

The uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (the Weierstrass scene). Show this fails for bounded variation: with g(x) = x^2\sin(1/x^2) for x > 0 and g(0) = 0, put
      \[g_n(x) = \begin{cases} g(1/n) & 0 \le x \le 1/n \\ g(x) & 1/n \le x \le 1 \end{cases}.\]
      (a) Show g is NOT of bounded variation on [0,1], using the oscillation at the points x_k = \sqrt{2/((2k+1)\pi)}. (b) Show each g_n is of bounded variation on [0,1] and g_n \to g uniformly.
